newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH TOURISM SURGES BUT VISTORS GO HOME SOONER.
newsitem.headline: CZECH TOURISM SURGES BUT VISTORS GO HOME SOONER.

text.p: The Czech Republic continued to attract tourists in record numbers in 1996, but they are staying for shorter periods of time hitting top class hotels and landlords, official figures released on Tuesday showed.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said the number of foreign visits, measured by border police, rose by nearly 12 percent compared with the 1995 to 109.4 million.
But a survey conducted by GfK Praha for the Czech Tourism Centre, showed a decline in the average length of stay in the country by tourists to 2.75 days from 3.09 in 1995.

"The average stay fell, above all, among tourists using rented apartments, rented rooms and hotels in the highest categories," it said adding there had been a corresponding rise in occupancy at lower accommodation categories.

Despite the bad news for hoteliers and landlords, the Czech government, which relies heavily on tourism revenues to help the country's balance of payments, can take heart from a rise in average daily expenditure to $35.02 from $29.54 in 1995.
Vistors also appear undeterred by the country's notorious reputation for a surly service culture and horror stories of dishonest taxi drivers, though the biggest complaint was against criminality.
The survey showed that approximately three quarters of foreign visitors in 1996 had been to the Czech Republic before with about half travelling here for their sixth or more trip.
While tourists worldwide continue to flock to the Czech Republic, Czechs themselves are travelling abroad in greater numbers.

Czech net toursim income, a major component in the country's balance of payments, is expected to fall to $1.1 billion in 1996 from $1.25 billion in 1995, the Ministry for Local Development said in January.
The fall in net income was attributed to a rise in the total amount spent by Czechs travelling abroad. In 1996, Czechs made 48.6 million foreign trips, up 8.3 percent from 1995, the CSU reported.

The Local Development Ministry said recently that total 1996 revenues from toursim should rise by 32 percent to $3.8 billion, while Czech spending abroad was seen rising by 65.6 percent to $2.7 billion.
